mcq.q: The model knows the policy but formats answers wrongly despite examples. Try…
mcq.why: Behaviour/format gaps are what supervised fine-tuning addresses.

mcq.q: What is the rule for moving up the adaptation ladder?
options: Start with fine-tuning to get the best result
Move up only when evaluation shows the current rung cannot meet the acceptance criteria
Move up whenever a new model is released
mcq.why: Each rung roughly multiplies cost, data needs and maintenance.
distractors: Fine-tuning before trying prompts wastes effort.
That is the most expensive rung.
Model releases are not evidence about your task.

mcq.q: Answers contain wrong or outdated facts with no citations. What is the likely remedy?
mcq.why: Missing or changing facts are a retrieval problem (9.1).
distractors: Too costly and still freezes facts.
Fine-tuning changes behaviour and freezes facts.

mcq.q: A large model does the task well but is too slow and expensive at your volume. What fits?
mcq.why: Generate verified teacher outputs on real inputs and fine-tune a small student.
distractors: That addresses domain language, not cost.

mcq.q: Distillation example: 3 million items a month at $0.004 each. What is the monthly cost?
Before distilling from a large model, what must you check?
options: That the teacher model's licence permits it
That the teacher is open source
That no human checks the outputs
mcq.why: Some licences restrict using outputs to train other models.
distractors: Hosted models can be teachers if the terms allow.
The student is smaller by design.

mcq.q: When is continued pretraining justified?
options: When the domain's language is far from general text and you have millions to billions of domain tokens
When answers are in the wrong format
When cost per call is too high
mcq.why: It is costly and needs SFT afterwards to restore instruction following.

mcq.q: A prompt needs 4,000 tokens of rules on every call. What does the chapter suggest?
options: Fine-tune the rules in and keep a short prompt
mcq.why: Fine-tuning can move stable behaviour into the model and cut prompt tokens.
distractors: Retrieval suits facts, not fixed behaviour.

mcq.q: Retrieval misses domain synonyms and codes. What is the likely remedy?
options: Fine-tune the embedding model or reranker
mcq.why: The miss is in the retriever, so adapt the retriever (13.5).
distractors: The generator cannot use evidence it never receives.

mcq.q: In the distillation case, the student was 1 point less accurate. Why was it accepted?
options: The team checked the drop was not concentrated on critical exception types
The student was always right on new data
mcq.why: An average drop is acceptable only if critical segments are not hurt.

interview.q: Walk through the adaptation ladder and when you would move up each rung.
How do you tell a retrieval problem from a behaviour problem?
What is distillation and when does it pay off?
Your team wants to fine-tune because answers are sometimes wrong. What do you ask first?
interview.followUp: What evidence would convince you to fine-tune?

interview.q: Build a business case for distilling a large hosted model into a small self-hosted one.
Why can fine-tuning to fix facts be a trap?
{company} extracts attributes from millions of seller titles. Which rung would you choose and how would you prove it?
interview.followUp: What would make you go back to a hosted model?

interview.q: Design a decision process a company can use for every adaptation request.

mcq.q: LoRA trainable parameters for one 4096×4096 matrix at rank 8?
What does LoRA train?
options: Two small matrices B and A whose product is added to a frozen weight matrix
mcq.why: The layer computes W·x + (α/r)·B·A·x with W frozen.

mcq.q: LoRA trainable parameters for a 4096 × 14,336 matrix at rank 8?
About how much training memory does full fine-tuning with mixed-precision Adam need per parameter?
mcq.why: Weights, gradients and optimiser state add up to about 16 bytes per parameter (6.6).

mcq.q: Using 16 bytes per parameter, about how much memory does full fine-tuning of an 8B model need?
mcq.why: 8 × 10⁹ × 16 bytes ≈ 128 GB, before activations.
distractors: That is roughly BF16 weights only.

mcq.q: What does QLoRA change compared with LoRA?
options: The frozen base is stored in 4-bit (NF4); adapters train in higher precision
mcq.why: This lets large models fit on a single GPU, at some speed cost.

mcq.q: After training, what can you do with B·A?
options: Merge it into W for no inference overhead, or keep it as a swappable adapter
mcq.why: Both options are available.

mcq.q: Where does most of LoRA's memory saving come from?
options: Gradients are not computed at all
Optimiser state is needed only for A and B
mcq.why: The frozen base needs no optimiser state or weight gradients.
distractors: Gradients flow through the base to A and B.

mcq.q: Few trainable parameters means low compute. True?
options: No; the frozen base still runs forward and backward on every step
mcq.why: Compute scales with the full model's forward and backward passes.
distractors: Compute is dominated by the base.

mcq.q: In the LoRA calculator, how does moving from q, v to all linear modules at the same rank change the trainable parameters?
options: It increases them, because more matrices get adapters
mcq.why: Parameters are summed over targeted matrices; all linear includes the large MLP matrices.

interview.q: Explain LoRA in simple terms, including the formula for trainable parameters.
Compare full fine-tuning, LoRA and QLoRA.
Why does LoRA save memory but not much compute?
How would you choose rank and target modules?
interview.followUp: What would make you go higher?

interview.q: Estimate the GPU memory to fine-tune an 8B model with full fine-tuning, LoRA and QLoRA.
When would you merge an adapter and when keep it separate?
covers: keep for many tasks on one base

interview.q: Design serving for {company}'s many task adapters on one base model.
interview.followUp: How would you roll back one adapter?

interview.q: Design a fine-tuning platform that lets teams train adapters safely on shared GPUs.

mcq.q: After fine-tuning, multilingual accuracy fell 7 points. You should…
options: Treat it as a regression gate failure and retrain with mixed data
mcq.why: General-capability regressions are release blockers when they breach the gate.

mcq.q: What is the honest baseline for measuring domain gains?
options: The base model with your best prompt
The base model with a weak prompt
mcq.why: A weak baseline exaggerates the gain.

mcq.q: What is catastrophic forgetting?
options: Loss of general capabilities after fine-tuning
mcq.why: Run general suites before and after; LoRA forgets less, but not nothing.
distractors: The opposite of memorisation, not forgetting.

mcq.q: How can you test for memorisation?
options: Prompt with prefixes of training records and check for verbatim completions; plant and probe canaries
Ask the model if it memorised data
mcq.why: Probes and canaries test extraction.

mcq.q: Can fine-tuning on benign data weaken refusal behaviour?
options: Yes; re-run safety and red-team suites on every fine-tuned model
No, only harmful data does that
mcq.why: Safety regressions are a known effect of fine-tuning.
distractors: Benign data can do it too.

mcq.q: In the scorecard, which gates fail?
mcq.why: Multilingual fell 7.3 points (limit 3) and refusal fell to 91.5% (gate 97%).

mcq.q: General instruction following fell from 81.0% to 78.5%. With a gate of “drop ≤ 3 points”, does it pass?
distractors: The gate is a drop, not a floor.
The gate allows up to 3 points.

mcq.q: Two gates fail on the scorecard. What does the chapter recommend?
options: Add multilingual and safety examples to the training mix and retrain
Ship to English users only without telling anyone
mcq.why: Fix the regressions, do not ship and hope.
distractors: Ship-and-hope is what the gates prevent.
Hidden restrictions are not a fix.

mcq.q: A few privacy probes find nothing. What does that prove?
options: The model is safe to release with PII
Only that those probes found nothing; it is not proof no data can be extracted
mcq.why: Absence of evidence from a few probes is weak; minimise PII in training data in the first place.

mcq.q: An adapter raises average field accuracy but begins inventing plausible IDs for missing fields. What should happen?
options: Block release; the fabrication gate matters more than the average
mcq.why: A higher average does not excuse a critical failure mode.
distractors: Removing the test hides the problem.

interview.q: What do you evaluate before releasing a fine-tuned model?
What is catastrophic forgetting and how do you detect it?
covers: LoRA reduces but does not remove

interview.q: How do you test a fine-tuned model for memorisation?
Your fine-tune improved domain accuracy but multilingual accuracy dropped 7 points. What do you do?
interview.followUp: What if the business wants to ship anyway?

interview.q: How would you set gates for a release scorecard?
A fine-tuned model refuses fewer harmful requests. Why might that happen and how do you fix it?
Design {company}'s pre-release checks for a model trained on customer text.
Design an evaluation pipeline that runs automatically on every fine-tuned candidate.

mcq.q: Which tends to produce a better fine-tuned model?
options: Tens of thousands of noisy examples
Any data, as long as there is a lot
mcq.why: The model learns whatever the data shows, including inconsistency.

mcq.q: What should a labelling guideline include?
options: Task definition, output schema, decision rules, worked examples, edge cases and what to do when unsure
mcq.why: A versioned guideline makes labels consistent.
distractors: A schema says what, not how to decide.
The prompt is not a labelling guide.

mcq.q: Two annotators have low agreement on a pilot. What should you fix first?
mcq.why: Low agreement points to unclear rules.
distractors: Fix the guideline, not the annotators.

mcq.q: Observed agreement is 0.90 and agreement expected by chance is 0.50. What is Cohen's kappa?
distractors: That is po − pe without dividing.

mcq.q: One annotator accepted 99% of model drafts unchanged while others edited 22%. What is the likely problem?
options: That annotator is the most skilled
The other annotators are too strict
mcq.why: Their accepted records had three times the error rate.
distractors: The others found errors to fix.
Higher acceptance came with more errors.

mcq.q: How did the team in the example detect rubber-stamping in future?
options: Hid the model draft for 10% of items (a blind check)
mcq.why: Blind items show whether an annotator really reads.
distractors: The fix was to the process.

mcq.q: When should the test set be split off?
options: First, before training, by customer or time if leakage is possible
mcq.why: Hold out the test set first and never train on it.

mcq.q: Choose all the automatic quality checks the chapter lists.
options: Contamination check against the evaluation set
mcq.why: Also PII scans and length or banned-content checks.
distractors: Hard cases are needed in the data.

mcq.q: What goes in a dataset's datasheet?
options: Sources, guideline version, annotator pool and known gaps
mcq.why: The datasheet documents how the data was made.
distractors: Personal details do not belong there.
Row count alone is not enough.

mcq.q: Where should inputs for a training set come from?
options: Real production traffic, privacy-reviewed, covering the real distribution plus hard cases
mcq.why: Real inputs match what the model will see.
distractors: Easy cases do not teach the hard ones.
Synthetic inputs can miss real patterns.
Benchmarks may not match your task.

interview.q: How do you build a fine-tuning dataset?
What is inter-annotator agreement and what does low agreement tell you?
Why can model-drafted labels be risky?
Your labelled data gives great test results, but production is worse. What could be wrong with the dataset?
How would you set up quality control for 10 annotators?
When do you stop revising a guideline and start scaling up?
Design {company}'s labelling process for a classifier with regulatory consequences.
interview.followUp: How would you handle a disagreement between experts?

interview.q: Design a labelling platform for several teams' datasets.

mcq.q: In extraction training data, why include many examples where a field is absent?
options: Otherwise the model learns to always fill fields
mcq.why: Without null examples, the model fabricates values.

mcq.q: In the contract example, only 2% of training examples had the termination clause absent. What happened?
options: The model invented a clause 31% of the time when none existed
mcq.why: Adding 600 absent-field examples brought fabrication to 2%.

mcq.q: For classification, what is often cheaper and as good as an LLM?
mcq.why: Small encoders classify well at a fraction of the cost.

mcq.q: Which domain-language adaptation has the highest regression risk?
options: Continued pretraining on domain text, then SFT
mcq.why: Mix in general data (e.g. 10–30%) to reduce forgetting.

mcq.q: When might constrained decoding be enough without training?
options: For structured output in an exact format
mcq.why: Constrained decoding (7.4) enforces the schema at generation time.
distractors: It does not teach which tool to choose.

mcq.q: Why do tool-use training records include the tool result turn?
options: So the model learns to use results, not only to call tools
Because the chat template requires it
mcq.why: The model must learn the whole loop.
distractors: The reason is learning to use results.

mcq.q: Choose all the evaluation measures listed for extraction.
mcq.why: Perplexity is for domain language, not extraction.
distractors: Listed for domain language, not extraction.

mcq.q: What should tool-use training data include besides tool calls?
mcq.why: Otherwise the model learns to call tools for everything.
distractors: Failures alone teach the wrong thing.
The calls and results matter too.

mcq.q: A fine-tuned model produces valid tool calls in the right format. Does that authorise execution?
options: No; authorisation and policy checks still apply
mcq.why: Training shapes behaviour; the runtime still checks every call (11.3).

mcq.q: Which chat template should tool-use fine-tuning use?
options: The template of a different model
The model's native tool-calling chat template
mcq.why: Matching the native template keeps the format the model and serving stack expect.
distractors: A different model's template does not match.
A custom template may break serving.

interview.q: How does training data differ for extraction, classification and tool use?
Why might a small encoder beat an LLM for classification?
What can go wrong when fine-tuning for extraction?
Your fine-tuned extractor reaches 97% field accuracy but users report invented values. How do you investigate?
interview.followUp: What metric would you gate on?

interview.q: How would you fine-tune a model for tool use?
When would you choose constrained decoding over fine-tuning for structured output?
Design {company}'s attribute extraction model: data, nulls, evaluation and release gates.
interview.followUp: How would you handle a new category?

interview.q: Design a fine-tuning approach for a tool-using agent, from data collection to evaluation.
covers: evaluate tool choice and final state

mcq.q: Why is fine-tuning the retriever often the highest-return adaptation in a RAG system?
options: General embedding models miss domain meaning, and retriever tuning is cheaper than LLM tuning
It removes the need for a reranker
mcq.why: Codenames, part numbers and terms of art are common misses.

mcq.q: What are hard negatives?
options: Passages that look relevant but are not, mined from the current model's top results
mcq.why: They teach fine distinctions and matter more than more easy pairs.

mcq.q: Why is a new reranker an easier first step than a new embedding model?
options: A reranker does not touch the index; a new embedding model needs a full re-index
mcq.why: Re-embedding means a blue/green migration (10.7).

mcq.q: Which loss is typical for embedding fine-tuning?
options: Mean squared error on token IDs
Contrastive loss with in-batch negatives (MultipleNegativesRankingLoss / InfoNCE)
mcq.why: It pulls queries and positives together and pushes negatives apart (4.4).

mcq.q: Where should you evaluate a fine-tuned retriever?
options: On real human queries with labels, not the synthetic ones you trained on
mcq.why: Synthetic training queries overstate gains.

mcq.q: A mined hard negative is actually a valid answer. What happens if you train on it?
options: The model learns to reject good evidence
mcq.why: Check mined negatives before training.
distractors: It hurts recall on similar queries.

mcq.q: In the synthetic pipeline, why filter generated questions?
options: To drop questions the chunk does not actually answer
mcq.why: A judge or round-trip check removes bad pairs.

mcq.q: Choose all the sources of (query, relevant passage) pairs the chapter lists.
options: Search logs with clicked or used results
mcq.why: Human labelling is another source.
distractors: Random pairs are not relevant pairs.

mcq.q: After fine-tuning embeddings for jargon, what should you also check?
mcq.why: Gains on jargon can come with losses elsewhere.

mcq.q: How are rerankers (cross-encoders) typically trained?
options: As binary or listwise classifiers over (query, passage)
mcq.why: They score each query–passage pair.

interview.q: Why fine-tune an embedding model or reranker instead of the LLM?
What are hard negatives and how do you mine them?
Explain the synthetic-data pipeline for retriever fine-tuning.
Recall improved on synthetic test queries but not on real ones. What went wrong?
interview.followUp: How would you collect real queries?

interview.q: When would you choose a reranker over a new embedding model?
How do you protect against false hard negatives?
Design retriever fine-tuning for {company}'s product search with shopper queries.
interview.followUp: How would you handle position bias in clicks?

interview.q: Design an ongoing process that improves a company's retriever from production feedback.

mcq.q: What should every training run log?
options: Config, code commit, dataset version, base model revision, hyperparameters, metrics and artefacts
mcq.why: Everything needed to rerun and trace it.

mcq.q: Why is exact bitwise reproduction often impossible on GPUs?
options: Non-deterministic GPU operations; aim for the same metrics within tolerance
mcq.why: Pin environments and seeds, record hardware, and compare within tolerance.
distractors: Seeds help but do not guarantee bitwise results.

mcq.q: What does a model registry provide?
options: Immutable versions and stages such as staging and production
mcq.why: Each version is traceable to its data and code.

mcq.q: Choose all the release criteria the chapter lists.
options: Approval by an owner and a rollback plan
The highest score on any benchmark
mcq.why: Release needs gates, documentation, approval and a way back.
distractors: A single benchmark score is not a release criterion.

mcq.q: What goes in a model card?
options: Intended use, training data summary, evaluation results, limitations and licence
mcq.why: It documents what the model is for and how it performed.
distractors: A name says nothing about use or limits.
Code is linked, not the card.

mcq.q: An adapter was tested on base revision A. Can it be deployed on base revision B without re-testing?
options: No; a different base revision requires re-testing
mcq.why: The adapter's behaviour depends on the exact base weights.

mcq.q: Which tools version datasets?
options: DVC, lakeFS or Hugging Face dataset revisions
mcq.why: Datasets need versions as models do.

mcq.q: Why record a model by immutable revision rather than by name?
options: Names can point to different weights over time
mcq.why: An immutable revision identifies exactly what was tested.

mcq.q: What should happen to the previous model version after promotion?
options: Be renamed to the new version
mcq.why: Rollback needs the previous version (18.4).

mcq.q: Which pins the software environment of a run most precisely?
mcq.why: A digest is immutable; tags can move.

What is a model card and what goes in it?
How do you trace a production model back to its data?
A retrained model scores lower and nobody knows why. How do you investigate?
interview.followUp: What would you add to prevent this?
